intro.heading: The shadow day went well. What did she actually learn?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care homes.
intro.paragraph: A new carer spends her first Tuesday shadowing a senior. She sees the morning routines, meets the residents and helps with a transfer under supervision. By the end of the shift she is smiling and the senior says she is a natural. The manager ticks the day off the induction list. A week later she is working shifts, and nobody has checked what she took in. Did she see how to handle a safeguarding worry, or which residents need thickened fluids? Watching is a start, not proof. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: The new carer shadows a senior through the morning routines.
She meets residents and helps with a transfer, with the senior beside her.
The senior says it went well. The manager ticks the day off the list.
She is working shifts, and nobody has asked what she understood.
The senior was busy and explained the fluids chart in a rush.
She is new, shy and keen to impress, so she nods instead of asking.
A tick and a kind word from the buddy. Nothing that shows understanding.
“How did you learn what to do when you started?” She cannot say.

trail_close: The shadow day was not the problem. The gap is between watching and knowing. Here is how CareStream fills it, using your own policies, without replacing the shift.

why.heading: Watching someone work is not the same as understanding the work
why.sub: A manager needs a way to see what each new starter took in, without a long chat for every person.

cards.title: New starters nod to fit in
cards.body: Many new carers will not say they missed something. They are shy, keen to impress, or English is their second language. A nod is not a check for understanding.

cards.title: Every buddy teaches differently
cards.body: One senior explains the reasons behind each task. Another just gets on with it. Two new starters can finish the same shadow shift knowing very different things.

cards.title: A tick on the list proves little
cards.body: A care home induction checklist records that the day happened. It does not show whether the carer understood safeguarding, fluids or what to do in a fire.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We already do a shadow day. Why add anything?
items.a: You would keep it. Watching a senior shows a new starter how your home runs. CareStream adds a short check afterwards, so you know what they took in, not just that the day happened.

items.q: How does the check work for a new carer?
items.a: After the shadow shift you allocate a short module on a topic, built from your own policies. They complete it in the Staff Hub on their own phone. Their answers are scored, so you can see who understood and who did not.

items.q: What happens when a new starter gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into their Follow-up tab and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need. You do not have to write or chase anything.

items.q: Will I be told every time someone gets an answer wrong?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the picture in the Knowledge gaps view in Analytics, and in a digest email on Monday. That shows whether one person needs a chat or your shadow shift needs a change.

items.q: Is the lesson generic, or about how we work?
items.a: It is built from your own policies where they cover the topic, with general good practice as the fallback. You can edit and preview the module before you allocate it.

items.q: Some of our new starters speak English as a second language. Does that help?
items.a: Yes, on the paid plans. A carer can open the lesson in their own language, so a wrong answer points to a gap in knowledge and not in vocabulary. The reminder emails stay in English.

items.q: Does this replace the Care Certificate or my sign off?
items.a: No. The Care Certificate needs a manager's observation and sign off, and CareStream does not do that for you. It checks understanding of your own policies and keeps the record. See our Care Certificate course if you want the standards online.

items.q: What does it cost to try?
items.a: There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans, and you can create a free account to look around first. Adhoc training is on the paid plans, so check the pricing page for what each includes.

cards.body: A new starter still needs to work beside an experienced carer and be observed doing hands on tasks. CareStream checks understanding. It does not watch anyone work.

faqs.heading: Staff induction and shadow days, answered

items.q: Is a shadow shift in a care home a legal requirement?
items.a: No. It is a common and sensible practice, not a rule in itself. What the regulations ask is that staff get the support and training they need to do the job. See regulation 18 on staffing, which says staff must receive appropriate support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal as is necessary for their duties.

items.q: How long should a shadow shift last in a care home?
items.a: There is no set length. Many homes use one to three shifts, then increase responsibility step by step. What matters is that the new starter is checked, not that a number of shifts has passed.

items.q: What is a check for understanding after shadowing?
items.a: It is a short set of questions that shows what the person took in. In CareStream you allocate a module on the topic, built from your own policies, and the new carer answers it in the Staff Hub.

groups.group: About induction and the Care Certificate

items.q: What should a care home induction checklist include?
items.a: Typically: a tour, key policies, fire safety, safeguarding, how to report concerns, residents' needs and who to ask. See our guide to the Care Certificate standards for the wider picture. CareStream does not replace your checklist, it adds a check on what they understood.

items.q: How does Care Certificate induction work?
items.a: The Care Certificate has 16 standards, and Skills for Care says they can be used to inform what is covered during induction. A manager or assessor with direct experience observes and signs off. Read how long it takes.

items.q: Can I use CareStream for agency staff induction?
items.a: Yes. Agency workers get time boxed access with no seat used on your plan, and are enrolled only in flows you mark as suitable for agency staff. See annual training for what comes later.

items.q: Does a knowledge check count as evidence for CQC?
items.a: It gives you a record of what each person was asked, what they got wrong and what they then learned. That sits alongside your other CQC evidence. It is not a substitute for observation.

guide.heading: A practical way to check understanding after a shadow day
guide.lede: Staff induction is more than the first shift. A shadow day is the moment a new starter sees your home in action, so it is the right moment to check what they saw and understood.

sections.h3: Make shadowing structured, not left to chance
paragraphs: Tell the buddy what to cover before the shift, such as the morning routine, how to report a concern and who needs help with fluids. Give the new starter a few minutes at the end to ask questions. The Skills for Care Care Certificate page says the 16 standards can be used to inform what is covered during induction, which is a useful guide for what a buddy should show.

sections.h3: Four checks that fit a busy home
checklist: Before the shift: brief the buddy on three or four things the new starter must see.
Within a few days: allocate a short check on those topics, built from your policies.
When an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each month: look at the most missed questions and adjust what your shadow shift covers.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the shadow day record, the check results and your sign off together, so you can show how each new starter learned the job.
